For Gram dimensions $d_1,d_2,d_3$, each level triple requires
$2d_1d_2d_3$ distinct vertex entries when $\eta=\eta'$ and
$4d_1d_2d_3$ when $\eta=-\eta'$, including both allowed parity
sectors. Successive Gram contractions and the final pairing use
$2d_1d_2d_3(d_1+d_2+d_3+1)$ complex multiplications. Distinct symmetric
Gram matrices require $d(d+1)/2$ entries each; $\sum d^3$ is an
inversion-cost proxy, not an exact operation count. The level-5 counts
agree with counters in the C++ run.

Vertex requests increase by a factor of 1,862 and contraction
multiplications by 16,605. Holding the measured C++ cost per entry or
product fixed, and scaling the other stages by their own work counts,
gives $6.55$ h and $8.54$ h. Vertex evaluation contributes $1.90$ h and $3.83$ h;
contractions contribute approximately $4.61$ h in each sector and dominate this baseline.
Unassigned internal work and process overhead, which include tensor and
cache destruction, are scaled by the vertex-entry ratio as a proxy.

A sensitivity scenario scales only the vertex cost further by the
entry-weighted mean total level, which increases from $11.71$ to
$25.02$, a factor of $2.137$. This illustrates the possible cost of
longer Ward recursions; it does not count their internal operations.
The two scenarios are neither runtime bounds nor a confidence interval.

The constant-unit-cost PBW estimates are about 57 and 19
times the measured C++ double-Virasoro wall times. This expected
advantage at level 10 is much larger than the measured level-5 advantage,
but no level-10 PBW run was performed. The 19-minute figure is a separate
projection from sampled Virasoro factors with the latest CCY changes,
weighted by the full branching workload; that full level-10 pipeline has
not been retimed. Equal working precision does not certify equal output accuracy.

\paragraph{Memory assumption.}
The estimates assume enough RAM to retain the caches without paging.
The current C++ Ward caches retain at least 659 million and 1.318 billion
distinct requested entries. Each has a 12-byte key within a 96-byte
key/value object and at least 48 additional bytes for the two 136-bit
mantissas on this platform. These objects and mantissas alone require
approximately 95 and 190 GB (decimal). Hash nodes, buckets,
additional internal Ward states, allocator overhead, mode-action caches
and tensor buffers add to this. No tensor-permutation tables are stored.
These are partial storage counts, not measured level-10 peak memory.
Insufficient RAM would require changing cache retention and re-estimating runtime.
